Notes

Topboy begins with domination but develops a more practical argument about protecting the ability to make things and choose companions. Its adversary depends on publicity and pleasing others; the speaker wants recognition without that dependence. Genuine friends remain a source of happiness, so walking alone is not the entire ideal. Wings and a safe turn caution into preservation of future freedom. The return to the opening boasts also keeps the contradiction alive: a song warning against attention's power still enjoys demonstrating who stands above whom.

xíng de duān

行得端、坐得正 declares upright conduct: one has done nothing shameful and can face scrutiny. After “stand high / see far,” its two clipped lines make physical posture and moral confidence share a rhythm. The speaker claims both the best vantage point and the right to judge what he sees.

  • Chinese lyric transcript (Genius community)
bié xiàn mù wǒ

Jackzebra named Top Boy among the shows he watches when discussing learning English through the internet in a 2025 Dazed interview. That gives the title a connection to his stated viewing habits. In this song, the opening claim to stand higher than everybody else also makes “top boy” function as a straightforward assertion of rank.

  • Jackzebra interview with Dazed (April 2025)
guān zhòng

The crowd supplies the opponent's humiliation while the speaker occupies the centre. In 'Throat', an audience similarly watched a performer suffer, but the vulnerable person was the speaker. Read alongside that song, this boast shows how easily spectatorship becomes a weapon when its target changes. The album does not offer one consistent position outside the cruelty of public attention; its voices can both suffer and enlist it.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
yí gè wèn hào

A question mark is something he can throw, and 接招 in the next line means receive or counter a move in a fight. Punctuation becomes a projectile. The boast is about making the other person answer on his terms: even confusion can be wielded as an attack rather than admitted as uncertainty.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
mài rén shè

Selling a persona is followed immediately by fear of being forgotten. The accusation is not simply that an image is constructed—this song plainly constructs one too—but that the other person has become dependent on keeping it in circulation. Pleasing everyone then appears as the work required to prevent disappearance. The boastful speaker wants to distinguish his own authority from that dependency, though his need to compare himself keeps the distinction under strain.

  • Chinese lyric transcript (Genius community)
yí wàng de dài jià

The accusation against selling a persona becomes a fear of disappearing from attention. That gives the insult a mechanism: pleasing this person and that person is driven by the terror of no one remembering you. The verse presents publicity as a dependency, with the carefully maintained image resting on fragile self-worth.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
zhǐ hú de chuāng

Traditional paper-covered windows supply a concrete image for the previous fragile self-esteem: one poke ruins the surface. The lyric moves directly from an abstract weakness to something that can be punctured.

  • Chinese lyric transcript (Genius community)
suì zuǐ de bā gē

八哥 is a myna, a bird known for imitating human speech. 碎嘴 means incessant, petty chatter. Together they reduce the opponent’s voice to tiresome repeated noise; the following charge that culture is “just talk” continues that attack on speech without substance.

  • Chinese lyric transcript (Genius community)
  • Taipei Zoo: mynas imitating human voices
pí hòu

皮厚 draws on 脸皮厚, a thick face: being shameless or unembarrassed when one should feel ashamed. English “thick-skinned” can praise resilience, but that is not the force of this insult. The accusation sits beside fragile self-esteem, so outward shamelessness and inward insecurity coexist.

  • Chinese lyric transcript (Genius community)
bèi cì guǐ

背刺 is a stab in the back, and by extension betrayal. Adding 鬼 turns the betraying impulse into a ghost; 上身 says it possesses the body. 随手做做 then treats that dramatic supernatural intrusion as something done casually. The line moves between a familiar social metaphor and a little horror scene.

  • Chinese lyric transcript (Genius community)
yí gè rén zǒu

“Now I see clearly” leads into walking alone, a connection heard repeatedly in this run of tracks: insight costs company. But 走到哪算哪 afterward gives the independence an improvised quality—go as far as one goes, work out the destination later. The refusal to join others does not require a finished plan.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
ròu biàn cài le

菜 can mean a dish or vegetables, but in competitive slang it also calls someone unskilled. 肉变菜了 keeps the literal kitchen picture—meat turning into a dish—next to the following refusal to keep playing. That juxtaposition allows competence and edibility to blur: the same word can put something on the menu or dismiss someone as an easy opponent.

  • Chinese lyric transcript (Genius community)
xiōng dì men guò de shùn

Happiness at his brothers' success interrupts the need to surpass an opponent. Here someone else's flourishing is not a threat. That moment prepares the warning against calling everyone a brother: the label matters because genuine mutual regard is valuable. The song is distinguishing chosen care from indiscriminate affiliation, rather than arguing that dependence on any other person is inherently degrading.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
tiān de zhǐ yì

Heaven's will is followed by equal effort, no free reward and a decision left to the listener. The lines distribute control instead of settling on either fate or total self-sufficiency. One cannot guarantee outcomes, but can still choose where to put work and whom to trust. That practical mixture is more useful to the song's later advice than treating the heaven line as a complete philosophy of resignation.

  • Lyric transcript (the passage discussed here)
tiān shàng bú huì diào xiàn bǐng

The proverb says that stuffed pancakes do not fall from the sky: rewards do not simply arrive without effort. Keeping the food image preserves the abrupt shift from heaven’s will to practical advice about working and deciding for yourself.

  • Chinese lyric transcript (Genius community)
chēng xiōng dào dì

称兄道弟 literally means address each other as elder and younger brothers; it describes proclaimed closeness between people who need not be relatives. After celebrating his own brothers’ good fortune, the speaker warns against granting that status freely. The following “sincerity doesn’t buy sincerity” questions whether the commitment will be returned.

  • Chinese lyric transcript (Genius community)
chì bǎng

The wings are to be protected before the opportunity to fly arrives; the ideas are stored before they can be taken or exploited. These are images of preserving capacity, not just hiding from people. The final claim that school does not teach this makes the verse into an alternative lesson about creative and social survival. Its horizon extends beyond winning the present argument to remaining able to act later.

About Jackzebra and this mixtape

Zhuang Zhuang Mixtape arrived on Surf Gang on October 2, 2026: 55 tracks, opening with Sour and closing with Sweet. Its cast widens from YoungQueenz on Poker Face to User116, Effie, kuru, yoyi, 春 and 南部犯罪份子. Aghast has a production credit on every track from Hitman through Snatch, giving that stretch a shared collaborator behind its changing scenes.

Surf Gang release · Artist credits

Jackzebra told AVYSS that he writes while singing over a beat he has listened to repeatedly, keeping the images in his head central. He values the room Mandarin leaves for indirect meanings. Listen for ordinary phrases becoming physical scenes: familiarity becomes cooking, authority becomes family seniority, and a tired saying suddenly turns into a threat.

AVYSS interview, 2024

In STATIC, he describes mixtapes as a format for letting ideas flow, reserving an official debut album for later. In a separate conversation about Above & Beyond, he compared that earlier tape to a collection of his producer friends’ work. The credits here likewise reward attention: long-running collaborators sit alongside guests working in Mandarin, Korean and English.

STATIC interview · Sabukaru interview, 2025

The small details connect to his stated interests: he has described playing Temple Run in transit and before shows, watching Top Boy, and wanting to score White Oleander. These give the songs specific points of contact with his life. The notes follow those connections alongside the lyrics’ jokes, invented scenes and competing voices.

His recommendations in Perfectly Imperfect · Dazed interview, 2025 · Interview questionnaire, 2025

Jackzebra has pushed back on being made to represent all of China’s underground. These notes stay close to the words: what an expression usually means, what changes in this line, and how another song answers it. Cultural references have sources; interpretations rest on details you can hear or read in the song.
